lesson.title: Flat Tangents: Solving f'(x) = 0
lesson.summary: The first and most common way a critical number arises is a horizontal tangent line, found algebraically by setting the derivative equal to zero and solving, sometimes by factoring and sometimes with the quadratic formula.
lesson.body:
Recall that a critical number can arise in exactly one of two ways: either f'(c) = 0, or f'(c) fails to exist. This section focuses on the first, more common, case. Geometrically, f'(x) = 0 means the slope of the tangent line at x is exactly zero, the graph is momentarily flat there, neither rising nor falling at that instant. That flatness is precisely the signature a smooth curve leaves behind at the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley, which is why solving f'(x) = 0 is the first move in almost every search for local extrema of a differentiable function.

In practice, once f'(x) has been computed, solving f'(x) = 0 is purely an algebra problem, and the right technique depends on what f' looks like. A quadratic derivative that factors nicely can be handled by factoring, as in the previous section. When a quadratic does not factor over the integers, the quadratic formula still works every time. Higher degree or more complicated derivatives may call for grouping, substitution, or graphing and numerical methods, but the goal is always the same: find every real solution to f'(x) = 0.

Try a case where factoring does not come easily. Let f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 2. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 3. Setting this to zero: 3x^2 - 6x - 3 = 0. Divide both sides by 3 to simplify: x^2 - 2x - 1 = 0. Look for two integers that multiply to -1 and add to -2, there are none, this quadratic does not factor over the integers, so reach for the quadratic formula instead. With a = 1, b = -2, c = -1, the formula gives x = (-b ± √(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a) = (2 ± √(4 + 4)) / 2 = (2 ± √8) / 2. Since √8 simplifies to 2√2, this becomes x = (2 ± 2√2) / 2 = 1 ± √2.

So the two solutions are x = 1 - √2, which is approximately -0.414, and x = 1 + √2, which is approximately 2.414. The domain of f is all real numbers, since f is a polynomial, so both irrational values are valid critical numbers. There is nothing wrong with a critical number that is irrational, the algebra simply has to be carried through correctly rather than forced into a factoring shortcut that was never going to work.

One useful fact falls straight out of this discussion: for any polynomial function, every critical number comes from this f'(x) = 0 case and none from the other case. That is because the derivative of a polynomial is always another polynomial, and polynomials are defined and differentiable at every real number, with no gaps, corners, or breaks anywhere. So the second doorway, a critical number arising from a derivative that fails to exist, requires stepping outside the world of polynomials, which is exactly where the next section goes.
